lessonRef.subject: financial-literacy
lessonRef.title: Explicit model: keeping money information private

standardsRefs: Manuel Academy Financial Literacy elementary sequence — Grade 3
Manuel Academy Financial Literacy G3 Unit 5 — money tools, privacy, and advertising
objective: Learners decide what money information is safe to share in an invented online game and identify who to bring a request to instead of answering it.
scenario: Amara is an invented third grader playing a pretend online game. A made-up in-game character asks her to type the long number from a family card so she can get a free pet. Nothing in this scenario is a real account, and no real number is ever typed anywhere.
safetyNotes: Every amount, person, business, and account in this task is invented for practice. Nothing here refers to a real household.
Never write a real bank account, card, PIN, password, Social Security, or tax number on this sheet; the task never asks for one.
This is education, not individualized financial advice. Real money decisions belong to a trusted adult.
Never type a real card, account, or password anywhere in this task; the scenario is invented and needs no real number.

tasks.directions: Read the invented in-game message with Amara. It offers a prize, it is friendly, and it asks for a number that belongs to her family. Sort what is being asked for before deciding what she should do.

prompts.text: What exactly is the invented game character asking Amara for, and who does that information really belong to?

tasks.directions: Amara has to answer the invented character. Write what she should do, and say what makes the friendly tone of the message unimportant to that decision.

prompts.text: What should Amara do about the request, and why does it not matter that the message sounded nice?

tasks.directions: Some information is fine to share and some is not.

prompts.text: Name one money thing that is fine to talk about at school and one that stays inside the family.

remediation: If a learner focuses on whether the prize is real, set the prize aside entirely and ask only who owns the number being requested, so the decision rests on ownership rather than on the offer.
extension: Ask the learner to write the exact words Amara could use to end the conversation and go find an adult.

targetConcepts.meaning: Money is limited, so choosing one use can mean giving up another use.
Needs, wants, goals, and constraints help explain why a choice fits a situation.
A sound choice uses the fictional facts without judging a person or family.

evidencePurpose: Develop and apply money choices and opportunity cost through the existing fictional lesson work, including calculation where relevant and evidence-based decision reasoning.

conceptExplanation.title: Understand money choices and opportunity cost
paragraphs: Money is limited, so choosing one use can mean giving up another use.

Needs, wants, goals, and constraints help explain why a choice fits a situation. In this lesson, the learner uses the provided fictional facts about keeping money information private; no real household information belongs in the work.

A sound choice uses the fictional facts without judging a person or family. The usable process is: Name the fictional goal. Separate needs, wants, and constraints. Compare the cost and the opportunity cost. Choose conditionally and support the choice with a scenario fact.
relationship: Compare the cost and the opportunity cost.
Choose conditionally and support the choice with a scenario fact.
conceptExplanation.commonConfusion: Calling an option a want does not make it bad; the category depends on the stated goal and circumstances.
conceptExplanation.conditionsAndLimits: Use only the stated fictional facts, time period, rate meaning, fees, taxes, timing, rounding, goals, and constraints. The result is education for this scenario, not individualized advice.

calculationPolicy.reason: The protected response contract is decision and judgment work; calculation is not manufactured merely to add arithmetic.

workedExamplePolicy.separationRule: The model uses different fictional people, amounts, wording, and decision conditions from protected independent and mastery work.

workedExamples.title: Worked example — money choices and opportunity cost
workedExamples.fictionCue: Every person, amount, product, institution, and rule in this example is invented for instruction.
facts: Imani has an invented $18.00 activity allowance.
workedExamples.goal: Keep the art project usable and decide what the remaining pretend money can cover.
workedExamples.relevantInformation: Use only the listed fictional facts and conditions; do not substitute real household information.
workedExamples.method: Name the fictional goal. Separate needs, wants, and constraints. Compare the cost and the opportunity cost. Choose conditionally and support the choice with a scenario fact.
steps: Represent $18.00 as 1,800 cents and $12.00 as 1,200 cents.
The $7.00 puzzle book costs 700 cents, which is 100 cents more than the $6.00 remaining.
Choose the board for the stated goal and delay the puzzle book; the opportunity cost is using $12.00 that cannot be used for another option.
workedExamples.interpretation: The choice follows the stated project constraint, not a claim that one kind of spending is always right.
workedExamples.reasonablenessCheck: Choose the board for the stated goal and delay the puzzle book; the opportunity cost is using $12.00 that cannot be used for another option.
workedExamples.tradeoff: If the board were already usable, the constraint would change and the puzzle book could be reasonable.
workedExamples.limits: The conclusion applies only to the stated fictional facts. A changed rate, fee, time, rule, goal, constraint, or risk can change it.
workedExamples.calculationAuthority: All USD calculations shown here are written as integer cents. Percent rates, when used, are integer basis points divided by 10,000; stated rounding is half up at the declared line only.

guidedPracticeContract.learnerAction: Identify the goal and constraints, compare alternatives, and support a provisional decision.
guidedPracticeContract.supportBeforeAction: Vocabulary, labelled facts, the approved separate model, and an empty organizer may be used only outside protected attempts.
guidedPracticeContract.feedbackAfterAction: Check for the observable confusion: Calling an option a want does not make it bad; the category depends on the stated goal and circumstances.
guidedPracticeContract.expectedEvidence: A learner-produced calculation or comparison plus financial meaning in the learner’s own words.
guidedPracticeContract.fade: Step cues and parallel models end before independent or protected evidence.

independentScenarioContract.independentBoundary: Use only the stated fictional facts and declared tools. No completed step, selected option, decisive justification, or protected result may be supplied.
independentScenarioContract.freshness: The protected case keeps the target but changes facts, constraints, timing, representation, or alternatives from the worked model.

decisionReasoning.gradeBandDemand: Name the goal, compare concrete costs or benefits, and explain one opportunity cost.
framework: Identify fixed facts, constraints, and assumptions.
Compare relevant benefits, costs, risks, and opportunity costs.
Use a calculation only when it answers a decision question.
Defend a conditional choice and name a changed fact that could change it.
decisionReasoning.neutrality: More than one conclusion may be defensible when priorities differ; scoring follows relevant evidence and internal consistency, not an adult lifestyle preference.

masteryRule.independenceRule: Worked examples, completed organizers, answer-bearing hints, or decisive feedback invalidate the protected attempt; use a fresh case after support.
masteryRule.evidenceRequired: A claim supported by relevant fictional evidence, tradeoff or risk reasoning, and acceptable variation under the adult-only rubric.
masteryRule.decisionRule: Mastery is decided only by the aligned adult-only authority for the named evidence lesson; completion alone is not mastery.

remediationRoutes.observableSignal: Calling an option a want does not make it bad; the category depends on the stated goal and circumstances.
remediationRoutes.alternateExplanation: Use a labelled fact–rule–result–meaning organizer. Separate what the fictional case states from what must be calculated or judged, then connect the result back to the stated goal.

parallelWorkedCase.title: Alternate model — money choices and opportunity cost
parallelWorkedCase.fictionCue: This is a different invented case, not a protected task answer.
facts: A bus pass for the fictional event is 900 cents.
parallelWorkedCase.representation: Write each money amount as integer cents, label the goal and constraints, and keep assumptions beside the calculation or comparison.
steps: Mark the bus pass as a constraint because it is required to reach the event.
Compare 600 cents remaining with the 800-cent souvenir; the gap is 200 cents.
Delay the souvenir and explain that the decision would change if transportation were already provided.
parallelWorkedCase.check: Reverse the arithmetic where possible and confirm that the conclusion uses a stated goal or constraint.

remediationRoutes.guidedRetryRule: Use the alternate representation on a different fictional case, require the learner to complete the decisive step, and fade labels after the attempt.
remediationRoutes.freshMasteryRule: Use a fresh protected case after support; do not count the parallel model or supported retry as mastery.

calculationPolicy.reason: The protected response contract is decision and judgment work; calculation is not manufactured merely to add arithmetic.

hintPolicy.mayReveal: Vocabulary, stated assumptions, relevant fact locations, and a non-protected parallel case.
hintPolicy.mustNotReveal: Protected results, winning options, decisive justifications, adult authority, or enough successive steps to reduce the response to copying.
hintPolicy.independenceEffect: A parallel worked case or answer-bearing help ends the current independent attempt and requires fresh evidence.

agePolicy.scaffolding: Use concrete choices, at most two interacting constraints at a time, short labelled cent calculations, and one evidence-based reason.
agePolicy.reasoningDemand: Name the goal, compare concrete costs or benefits, and explain one opportunity cost.
agePolicy.privacy: Never request real household income, debt, balances, spending, tax records, credit data, credentials, or hardship information.
agePolicy.adviceBoundary: Discuss only approved fictional cases and general educational questions; do not direct real financial action.

answerPolicy.authority: adult-only companion scoring artifact resolved by stable package and prompt references
answerPolicy.revealRestriction: No protected fixed answer, rubric locator, or scoring trace appears in the learner package.
answerPolicy.workedExampleSeparation: Learner-visible examples are separate instruction and never authority for protected task responses.

accessibilitySupports: Use concrete choices, at most two interacting constraints at a time, short labelled cent calculations, and one evidence-based reason.
Read-aloud, vocabulary clarification, labelled text representations, calculator use when declared, and an unfilled organizer may reduce access burden without performing the target work.
Color, audio, spatial arrangement, and drag interaction are never the sole carrier of a required financial fact.
